Your Honours, for your ease in going through her testimony, we have provided a chart that shows the order in which exhibits will be presented to her today. And then another column indicates the exhibit number of that exhibit in her prior testimony, because the Judges and the Defence have her prior testimony, we thought, perhaps, that would be helpful for the Judges and the Defence to have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if you'll hand that up, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we previously provided a similar list to the Defence. However, for them, we have added another column that gives them the number of previously disclosed evidence to them where it corresponds to these exhibits. JUDGE HANNE SOPHIE GREVE

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Will you please state your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a lawyer and, at the moment, I am a judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And how long have you held your current position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have been the President of the Court of Appeals, which in my system also includes functions of a high court for Western Norway for the two last years. And I have been a judge in the same court for the eight previous years.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And you have been chosen for what position in the future?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was selected in January of this year as a Judge to the European Court for Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And when will you assume those duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1st of November, this year.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Judge Greve, at this time, I would like to provide you Prosecution Exhibit 8. This is a curriculum vitae that has been previously provided to the Defence and to the Judges. Is that your curriculum vitae?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is my curriculum vitae, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, we would offer that into evidence as Prosecution Exhibit 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Judge Greve, were you appointed to a United Nations Commission of Experts concerning the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was back in October of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And did you subsequently write a report on the events in Prijedor in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote that report in 1994 and made a final version in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And by what mandate or resolution were you appointed to the Commission of Experts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came in as my predecessor died. But the resolution that was the basis for the Commission, was a Security Council resolution, which was made in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: At this time, I would like to show the witness what has been marked as Prosecution Exhibit 9 for identification. It's a copy of resolution 780. And what is that resolution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the Security Council resolution of the United Nations which establishes or mandates the Secretary-General to establish a Commission of Experts.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And looking at that resolution, what is the mandate given this Commission of Experts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's listed under Roman Number II, "Requests the Secretary-General to establish as a matter of emergency, an impartial Commission of Experts to examine and analyse the information submitted pursuant to a resolution 771, 1992, and a present resolution, together with such further information as the Commission of Experts may obtain to return investigations or efforts of all the persons or bodies pursuant to resolution 771, 1992, with a view to providing the Secretary-General with its conclusions and the evidence of grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions and other violations of other humanitarian law committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, we would offer Prosecution Exhibit 9 for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We take it there is no objection unless you say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Judge Greve, when did you complete your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was completed with names in it, actually in June 1994. But for publication purposes, we took out names and the final version was made, Easter 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would like to provide you with what's been marked as Prosecution Exhibit 10 for identification. And I would note, Your Honours, that the Judges and the Defence counsel have previously been provided with a copy of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, there is no need to provide another one.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you would just show that to the Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANN
utterances.text: We object to the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You object?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the ground of the objection, Mr. Vann?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the grounds of the objection is twofold. The most important of which is, as Your Honour stated earlier, I think this is an exhibit that Your Honour said that contains multiple hearsay and otherwise inadmissible evidence. Primary objection to this exhibit, that it constitutes the very foundation of the Prosecution's case. We've all had a copy of that exhibit. It is filled in drips with ideological venom that's now been spread by virtue of the opening statement throughout the world. There is no way that we can cross-examine these statements. There is no way. There is no way that we can cross-examine the judge here. Because she has no personal knowledge of any of the statements in this exhibit. In essence, we are being denied the fundamental right that's recognised in any court under principles of international jurisprudence of the right to cross-examination and the right to confront witnesses in open court to determine the credibility that these witnesses, when they are present, to be subject to cross-examination. It is a very, very difficult task, indeed, for a lawyer to cross-examine the foundation of the State's or Prosecutor's case without being capable of doing so. We have been effectively cut off to cross-examine anything in this case. Your Honour knows, all of you know, that the honourable Judge with her excellent credentials, there is no way we can cross-examine because she's merely a conduit. And, as the prosecuting attorney has said, she has summarised, analysed and collated information from 400 witnesses. This constitutes the very heart and soul of the prosecuting attorney's case. That is totally unfair and in any court, in any civilised society, to have a man's life depend on multiple hearsay where the defendant is being denied the essential right that any accused has in any trial to have him convicted on the type of evidence that they're trying to introduce at this time, which gratuitously contains slanders against the people, the Serb people. Contains slanders against one of their most revered generals in history, Drazan Mihajlovic. This type of poison inserted in the record is going to incite others who have listened to this and will listen to it over the Internet and anywhere else in the press. We're here to temper that type of action. Hopefully to try this case on the merit. To keep the attacks based on hearsay to a small level and to have a judgement based on impartial evidence without inflaming anybody. Your Honour knows the character and the type of witness that's in this document. It violates the fundamental rights of cross-examination and the right to confront witnesses. Further, Your Honour, with reference to an expert witness, they cannot merely summarise evidence and introduce it under the guise of being an expert. And for those two essential reasons, we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Hollis, what basis are you seeking to put this report before us?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're seeking to put it before you on the basis that we set forth when we responded to the only Defence motion that has been raised until now regarding this witness. And that had to do with wanting the notes of the 400 witnesses, so that they had the right to confront them or to confront this witness about those notes. Until today, the Defence has made no objection to this report itself. Rather, has simply requested that they be allowed to be provided notes that this witness took contemporaneous with her interviews of witnesses. The Trial Chamber disposed of that motion earlier and denied that motion. So we're somewhat surprised by this objection to the report. As we stated in our earlier response, the report is submitted as a part of the expert statement that this Trial Chamber requested at an earlier status conference, that both sides would provide such a statement to the Trial Chamber and then the opposing party had a certain period of time to object to the statement. We would suggest that in regard to the substance of the report itself, that it is very clear on its face, she does not purport to give exact details from specific witnesses. What she purports to do in that report is to analyse a great body of evidence. And, based on that analysis, reach certain conclusions. It's in a summary form, such as a contemporary historian may provide when reviewing evidence that occurred very recently. The Trial Chamber earlier today has noted that it fully understands the nature of this report and the nature of her testimony. And that the nature of the report and testimony would go to the weight of that testimony. And that is how it was presented before we adjourned for lunch. In regard to the objection concerning hearsay, first of all, we would point out, and as the Court well knows and as the Defence well knows, there is no rule in this Tribunal which prohibits the admission of hearsay evidence. The rule is rather, what is the relevance of the evidence? What is the probative value? If it is hearsay, it may be of such a nature that the Court would ultimately conclude there are not sufficient guarantees of trustworthiness to allow that particular piece of evidence in. But it would not be based upon a general prohibition against hearsay that does not exist in this Tribunal. Again, we would suggest it goes to the weight of the testimony to be afforded with this witness. Therefore, Your Honours, we provided it as a summary based on an extensive analysis of documents, performed in her capacity as an expert appointed by the United Nations to review the events in this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you want to add anything, Mr. Vann?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, what we're doing here and what we're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you mind being on your feet?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The Prosecution hasn't answered our question and that is, our objection is mainly viewed on the general principle of general jurisprudence that we cannot cross-examine any witness. Those witnesses are not here. We're not talking about simply hearsay that an expert may use to fortify their expert opinion. We're talking about being denied the right to cross-examine a paper witness. We cannot cross-examine a piece of paper, 600 or whatever amount of pages in this record or this tendered exhibit, is nothing more than a paper witness. It's not this witness that is testifying. She has no knowledge of any fact contained in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I repeat what I said earlier when dealing with this witness' evidence and commenting on it. It is our view that the witness should be treated as an expert in this sense, an expert who has made a study of material and is therefore qualified to give evidence about it. The position being analogous to that of the historian. We take entirely the point made by the Defence, that they cannot cross-examine the 400 witnesses on whose statements this evidence will be based. We understand that. But in this Tribunal we admit all types of evidence. The hearsay rule does not apply, but the issue of how much weight is given to this evidence is very much a matter for the Tribunal. And, in that connection, we shall, of course, bear in mind that it is hearsay. And, as I said earlier, sometimes hearsay upon hearsay. With those considerations in mind, we shall admit this report. But, I should make it quite plain, there is no question of this defendant being convicted on any count on the basis of this evidence. And we shall require other evidence before we consider taking any such course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could I ask you, Dr. Greve, how it was that you were chosen to act as a rapporteur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, is your question related to how within the Commission I was asked to act as rapporteur?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: How you personally were chosen, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came into the Commission rather late for the reason my predecessor died. And when I joined the Commission, there were already a number of studies being made. A lot of information was being gathered. I thought, having lived in areas, conflict areas before, that if I could be of any help to the Commission, at what time it was not yet sure whether we would continue to work for two and a half months, half a year or nine months and we only worked half time for the Commission, I should try to look at a limited area to see if there was any basis for a number of allegations at that time made. Having lived in conflict areas, I know very well that rumours feed very well in such circumstances. And I thought that in order to be able to distinguish between what merely would be rumours and what, perhaps, would be substantial, I needed to limit my study. I asked the Commission at first if I could make a study of a small area that had been attacked by the Croats. What then happened was that was at the end of one of our sessions. We had a fortnight when we were working in our home countries. Before we were meeting the next time, I was called by the Russian secretary to the Commission and he told me that in Sweden, and the Swedish and Norwegian languages are quite similar, there had been made a number of interviews with refugees from the former Yugoslavia. And as I would be able to read through this, would I be kind enough to go via Sweden and read those interviews? Which I did. Then I did see that a number of the people who had been interviewed in Sweden were from the Prijedor area. And they were coming up with strong allegations of much violence. Coming back to the Commission, I thought as we were short of time, perhaps it would be valuable if I could focus on the area of Prijedor, so that we didn't have to wait for all these statements to be translated into English. It was approximately, or close to 30 statements that related to Prijedor. And I asked the Commission if I could be mandated to try to make a study of the area of Prijedor and that was accepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And how long did you work on that project?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did work on it from late November. We submitted our first summary analysis the 1st of May, 2nd of May, the next year. And then the final version was ready by mid-summer, 16th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And of what year was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you testify before a Trial Chamber of this Tribunal in the case of the Prosecutor vs. Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: At this time I would like to provide you with what has been marked as Prosecution Exhibit 11. Your Honours, this has previously been provided to the Trial Chamber and to the Defence. Would you please show that to the Defence? Dr. Greve, have you had the opportunity to review that prior to coming in here to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And is that your testimony in the case of the Prosecutor vs. Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Prosecution would offer that as Prosecution Exhibit 11. Dr. Greve, once you were chosen to be a member of the Commission of Experts, what did you do to give yourself some background of the task before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I tried to read whatever general statements had been made by international agencies. And I tried to start reading information that had been gathered already by the Commission, which had been working then for a little more than one year.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what types of sources did you review in carrying out your task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, initially, I started with some of the main agencies, UN reports, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the Conference then on Security and Cooperation in Europe. And a variety of sources that had been gathered by the Commission as such. But I did not specify on any particular area. I tried to get a view of the overall situation. I should add that at the time when this was happening, I lived in Cambodia, working for the United Nation Transitional Authority in Cambodia. I came to Cambodia in August, 1992, and I only returned early spring 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: At this time I would like to show you a document we would ask be marked Prosecution Exhibit 12 for identification. Could you tell us what is this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a statement made of the President of the International Committee of the Red Cross, Mr. Cornelis Sommaruga. It is a statement which he gave in Geneva on 29th of July, 1993. It was a conference which was convened by the High Commission for Refugees, the United Nations High Commission for Refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And is that one of the documents that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And if you could turn to page 2 of that document, please. Looking at the 4th paragraph, beginning with the word "behind", what does that document indicate about the term "ethnic cleansing"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's indicating that so-called ethnic cleansing is going on, on a large scale and that with horrifying consequences for the people.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And if you could look at the next paragraph of that document. What does the document indicate concerning the status of victims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is suggesting that numerous victims are civilians who take no part in the hostilities. And, therefore, are especially vulnerable.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And if you could, please, also look at page 4, the second paragraph of that document, which begins "more generally". What is the indication there of the frequency of breaches of International Humanitarian Law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's suggesting that the breaches are very, very frequent.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And Dr. Greve, these portions to which you have been referred, are those consistent with your analysis that you undertook?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We would offer the document as Prosecution Exhibit 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sorry for the pause. In our system we would be listening to whether the Defence objects or not. I'll get better with the procedure as we go by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I imagine you will hear from them if they do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: At this time we would like to provide the witness what we would ask be marked as Prosecution Exhibit 13 for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an appeal made by the International Committee of the Red Cross to all parties in the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina to abide by basic standards and the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you would look at the first paragraph of the document. What does it indicate concerning the treatment of civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is suggesting that innocent civilians are being arrested and subjected to inhumane treatment. Moreover, the detention of such persons is part of a policy of forced population transfer carried out on a massive scale, and marked by the systemic use of brutality. Among the long list of matters used are harassment, murder, confiscation of property, deportation, and the taking of hostages, which would use individuals to the level of bargaining counters, all in violation of international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And considering that statement, in light of your analysis and conclusions, is that consistent with your analysis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is consistent.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We would offer the document as Prosecution Exhibit 13.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, I would now like to show you what we would ask be marked as Prosecution Exhibit 14 for identification. What is that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a document from the then CSO conference, Organisation on Security and Cooperation in Europe. It's a committee of senior officials.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And did you review that document in the course of your preparations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And if you could look at paragraph 2 of that document, please, near the bottom of the paragraph. What is the reference there to the Yugoslav National Army or JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's stated that despite a new agreement on a cease fire, there has been a continuous extension of the conflict on an unprecedented scale, including two other parts of the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and involving different parties. In particular, there has been a relentless attack on Sarajevo and continuous fighting elsewhere, with use of air force and heavy weaponry by the Yugoslav National Army, JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And in paragraph 4 of that document, what is the reference there to the involvement of Belgrade and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's suggesting strong involvement. The pattern of clear, gross and uncorrected violations of OSCE commitments by the authorities in Belgrade and by the JNA is now unmistakably established. Those leaders have driven themselves into isolation. It is they who bear the prime responsibility for the escalation of bloodshed and destruction.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And regarding the involvement of the JNA, is that consistent with your analysis based upon your study?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The only thing that differs is that in the Prijedor area there were no such use of the air force in the main attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We would offer that as Prosecution Exhibit 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, as to the foundation of this document. It doesn't indicate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you've got an objection, on your feet, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence objects to introduction of the CSO declaration of Bosnia-Herzegovina because we don't have a foundation here propounded what CSO is, what were the duties at the time in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Were those duties overlapping with the duties of some other international bodies? Was it a political mission? Was it a military mission? What methods did they use to study? They are concentrating basically on Sarajevo and other areas? The objection is also tied in conjunction to testimony of Judge Greve when she noted in her report to the Secretary-General that the military observers of the United Nations were withdrawn from Banja Luka area on April 28, 1992, because it was too dangerous. So we would like to know, is this an office report or any report that's worth considering. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's our position, that sufficient foundation has been established for this report. The witness has indicated that she did use it in her review and preparation for her tasking. We had provided a description of the exhibits indicating that this particular exhibit was taken from “Yugoslavia through Documents, from its Creation to its Dissolution”. Therefore, we feel that an adequate foundation has been laid for this document and the Defence's objection would basically go to the weight of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in addition, I have additional -- Your Honour, I have additional objection to this document. Because this document on its face indicates it's a document for a CSO, an international organisation which Prosecution is using to prove their case-in-chief. Just recently this Trial Chamber has decided that it does not have power to issue subpoena and that Defence Counsel are deemed as individual members of the public general, I think, and therefore access to CSO documents have been denied to them. To admit this document or any reference in this would obviously be a violative principle of the quality of arms. And, moreover, Your Honour, if indeed this document is admitted, I would like you to reconsider your previous decisions in relating to Defence access to this -- to the documents of this organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll admit this document. It's the views of diplomats, apparently, but what weight we give it, of course, is entirely for us to decide. And we'll have that in mind when we come to consider it. Ms. Hollis, it may be that someone should find out exactly who CSO is. We think it's the Committee of Senior Officials of that organisation. Perhaps the judge can help us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Forgive me if I didn't state that clearly. That is the interpretation, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, we'll admit that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Judge Greve, you indicated that you were chosen to work on the events in the Opstina or Municipality of Prijedor. At this time, we'd like to show you what we would ask be marked as Prosecution Exhibit 15 for Identification. Could you tell us what that is, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a map of the former Yugoslavia where also the municipality or the town of Prijedor, in particular, is marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And in what part of Bosnia-Herzegovina is Prijedor located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prijedor is located in the north-western part of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would offer Prosecution Exhibit 15 for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Judge Greve, in your report at paragraph 43 you discuss the importance of Prijedor in terms of its location in a corridor. Could you tell us what the significance of that corridor is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this time, if I may make reference to the map which has just been handed out. Vojvodina, Serbia, Montenegro, Kosovo, is all almost functioning as one entity. And in Croatia there are four areas at this time which have been so-called ethnically cleansed: Eastern Slavonia, Western Slavonia, and an area in Knin. Save for the area in Eastern Slavonia, and there will be another map to show it exactly, the areas in Knin and in Western Slavonia are not linked to the area of Serbia and the republics together with Serbia. So in order to connect the two, there had to be a corridor, or a linkage. And that could best be made through the northern part of Bosnia. So in any understanding of a corridor linking the areas in the Croatian part of Krajina, I should say Prijedor is the Bosnian part of Krajina, and also the Western Slavonian area in Croatia with Serbia, Montenegro, Vojvodina and Kosovo, there had to be a corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we do not have a map that shows the lines of communication, but perhaps you could tell us, what is the significance of Prijedor in this corridor concerning lines of communication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prijedor may be described as an intersection. There is a main road going from Banja Luka, which is not on this map either, but which is not so far from Prijedor. It's a bit to the east and south of Prijedor, which runs the whole way to the Croatian border. And there is also another main road which links Prijedor with a border town north of Prijedor, on the border of Croatia, and runs through Prijedor to the south, to the Sanski Most area. And there is a railroad which connects Banja Luka-Prijedor and runs all the way to Zagreb. It was not necessary for the corridor to have it all the way to Zagreb, but it is a very important quality of Prijedor, that it's traffic, it's an intersection for traffic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We would offer Prosecution Exhibit 16 for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We are on 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: 15 for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness has testified, and the Prosecution has stated in response to our motion, that Judge Greve doesn't have any personal knowledge of events in Prijedor, that she has not travelled there, that, to the best of my recollection, that she has not travelled to former Yugoslavia. And this Court, this Tribunal, this Trial Chamber, has given us instruction at the beginning that Judge Greve is going to merely testify as a contemporary historian. However, now she's testified not only outside the geographical area that she has interviewed, basically which she stated the only narrow area of Prijedor. She has testified that there was ethnic cleansing, the area others were ethnically cleansed, Western Slavonia, Eastern Slavonia, and Croatian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, let me interrupt you. We are not concerned with that evidence. She could give evidence, it seems to me, the witness, if you'll give -- the witness can give evidence about the geography. If you dispute it, you can cross-examine her. That seems to me it's probably fairly undisputed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I am addressing is extremely prejudicial to our client to allow the witness to submit the evidence of which she doesn't have any personal knowledge, or she has not investigated, and has nothing to substantiate this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: She has got sufficient knowledge to give some evidence about the geography. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: At this time I would like to show the witness what we would ask be marked as Prosecution Exhibit 16 for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, could you tell us first what that is a map of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a map which is indicating the military situation at one time, but that is not the reason why I have asked to have this marked. The reason why this map is being presented is that it was the only map I could find where the outlines of the four United Nation protection forces zones were clearly marked: Eastern Slavonia, Western Slavonia, North and South and Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And in terms of the corridor, what is the significance of those zones to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason why this has been also marked, it was only the marker at hand, was yellow. No significance to the colour. I have tried to mark the --

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps at this time we could fold the map and put it on the overhead projector to aid the witness as she testifies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What may be seen here is Eastern Slavonia, which borders Vojvodina and Serbia proper, and it comes further down, and all this eastern part is coloured yellow. It means it's all related to Serbia. What will be seen then is that Western Slavonia is sort of without linkage to Eastern Slavonia. And also the two other areas north and south of Krajina has no linkage. And I think this is the best I can do to see both sides at the same time. There has to be -- if there is to be physical contact between the two areas, there has to be some kind of a corridor that connects them. Of course they could be connected only by air or something like that. But if there is to be a geographical linkage, it has to be somehow through Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The areas that are marked in yellow, are these the Serb areas you referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are the Serb areas I referred to earlier, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And if you could, while you have the map on the overhead, if you could in general show the Trial Chamber where this corridor that you have talked about would run.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, the corridor will run in the very northern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and here in the western part it would be wider. But you will see here, where we see Prijedor, it's quite clear here that it functions like an intersection with some main roads, one going east-west, one going, more or less, north-south. And this is Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would offer that as Prosecution Exhibit 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we object on this one. With all due respect to Judge Greve, but the map is rather detailed. It shows the certain areas where the United Nations forces were stationed or were about to be stationed at the time that this map was made. However, the Prosecution has not presented Judge Greve neither as an expert in military affairs, nor expert in political affairs. And the concept "corridor" has been introduced. There is absolutely no foundation what is a corridor all about. That's number one. But, most importantly, objection to the very -- to the very map, the exhibit. There is no corridor that's being, you know, introduced here. I mean, there was some conjecture, what a corridor should be, or it was, and perhaps the corridor related occurred, but much later as a result of the military activities. However, we have to tie it up geographically, and in time in order for this exhibit to be admitted. I do not object to this map being re-drawn and corrected, but we cannot cross-examine based on this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One aspect of this map, Ms. Hollis, which does appear to be objectionable, the notes at the bottom, assessment notes, legend, and all the rest of it. Now, I haven't read those in any detail, and I don't propose to, and that we would rule inadmissible. But as for the rest of the map, I think we will admit it on this basis: That it's purely a map. Whether there's a corridor attached or not will depend upon the evidence that we hear. We'll have to make a judgement whether that assertion is justified or not. At the moment it can be no more than an assertion. So we admit the map as a map. We disregard entirely everything on the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: With the Trial Chamber's permission, we will redact the material that you have mentioned, and provide a substituted map with that material taken off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll return these maps meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would like to provide the witness with what we would ask be marked as Prosecution Exhibit 17 for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this is, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a newspaper article. It has been translated from the Serb language. It's from a newspaper called Kozarski Vjesnik. It's the daily newspaper or the main newspaper in Prijedor, and it's an article written 1st of July, 1994. It's headlined "The glory of all Serb glories."

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you could turn to page 2 of that article, please. And if you could look at the section entitled "Survival on native soil made possible." In that part of the article whom are they quoting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are quoting Colonel Radmilo Zeljaja. Oh, sorry. This is from the telegram of the commander of the general staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And on that page what is the reference to a unified Serb state? If you will look at the bottom of that section beginning with "congratulating you."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "I recognise the results achieved up to now and invite you to persist in achieving your freedom and the creation of a unified Serb state by maintaining a high level of combat readiness of our units, and safeguarding our front lines, and through strong morale and unity of the people and army and I wish St. Vitus Day to be celebrated in peace in the years to come."

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you could look below that under "loyal followers of Serb heroes" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We are quoting another person, and the article is quoting another person, commander of the First Krajina Corps, General Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And if you could look at the last paragraph on that page. What is indicated there about a corridor, in quotes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "In just two years, after successful battles in Western Slavonia, Kordun, Banija and Lika, the units of the First Krajina Corps began battle and an operation in the region of north-western Bosnia in order to protect the Serb population, liberate the territory from the enemy and provide conditions for the creation of a Serb state in this region. In the operation to open the so-called corridor, that natural and genetic artery of the Serbs in all three Serb states, the fighters from the Corps supported," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And in regard to "the fighters from our corps", who does General Talic indicate supports those fighters of the corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is suggesting that institutions of civil authority and the Serb people are supporting them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And if you could please look at the last page of that document. And what is said there about a road of life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "By making the road of life real, linking us again with our parent state and the native country of the Serb people, the Republic of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia with a strong demonstration of the Serb pride." Then it's stated that they have created conditions for re-creation of the Serb state in these regions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated earlier that this was an article in Kozarski Vjesnik, and that was, I believe you indicated, that was a newspaper. That was a newspaper where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Opstina Prijedor. It was the main newspaper in Opstina Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We would offer this as Prosecution Exhibit 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, according to the list that we have already, 17 should be a current situation map.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Because we were unable to get the map for the lines of communication, we are one behind the order that we gave you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, would it not be more sensible to stick to the original pagination and make this 18?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And then, Your Honour it would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Seventeen can be left blank for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: It would be Prosecution Exhibit 16, would be not offered, that is a map showing lines of communication in northern Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So this will be 18; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANN
utterances.text: Are they offering it in evidence, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there an objection to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANN
utterances.text: Yes. Relevancy to the matters that the Court has considered in this case about the unified Serb state, the defendant here is being tried with matters that are completely not germane. I don't know what the injection of this -- unless counsel deems it's inappropriate and wrong to have the Serbs to have their own nation and everybody else can have it but the Serbs. But I don't know what the relevancy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think that's the point at all. I think the point that's being made is to do with the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. At this time we would ask the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 19.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, what is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is again a newspaper article from the same newspaper from Opstina Prijedor, the paper Kozarski Vjesnik dated 15 July 1994. It's headlined "Faithful to the homeland and its ideals." It's a speech which is given on the occasion of the ceremony commemorating the birth of the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you will please look at page 1, the second full paragraph. In that paragraph it is indicated that the SDS was created how many years earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. It's founded in Sarajevo four years earlier. 15 July 1990 that would be, on the day of the holy apostle.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you could please look at page 3 of that document, the first full paragraph toward the end of that paragraph. What is said about a corridor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We are talking about page 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The first full paragraph beginning "having decided". If you could look at the end of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's stated that, "'The word corridor is too weak to describe that bond. The neck is not a corridor between the head and the body. It is all one being, the being of the Serb nation,' said the top man of the Prijedor SDS categorically."

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And if you could please look at that same page, page 3, the second line of that paragraph with the word "Turkish state." If you know, to what group would that term "Turkish" refer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have been told that that is being used for the Muslims, and that is how it comes through in written reports as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, just a moment. Does that appear in the document, "Turkish is derogatory for Muslim among Serbs." Is that in the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: That, Your Honour, we believe is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it shouldn't be here. We'll cross it out. We require that documents are translated as they appear, without any form of comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Judge Greve, based upon your analysis of that area and the events of that area, what, if anything, did your analysis disclose was the nature of Turkish, when being referred to Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Turkish was used on several occasions --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, this is not in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can give evidence about this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If, I may, Your Honours, take your attention to the 4th line, before what is not in the document, it's stated, "A new Turkish State, began to create a state entity", et cetera, so the word "Turkish State" is used in the document, but not the explanation which has been included in the translation here. And Turkish is frequently used with a reference to the Muslims, but they are also South Slav, people of the South Slav ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, if you would please turn back to page 2 of that document. And if you would look at -- under the section "For the Good of the People". The second paragraph under that section, beginning from the very start. Do you notice the reference to the Krajina SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There is -- there is a special reference. This is, therefore, the occasion to remind ourselves of the visionary programme of the Krajina. That is, in this case, the Croat Krajina, SDS, and its leader Jovan Raskovic. That's also a Croat leader, Croat Serb leader.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And if you will look at the next paragraph, please. What is the indication of the association between the SDS and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's suggesting there are strong ties between the two and they are working in tandem.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We would offer the document into evidence, Your Honour, as Prosecution Exhibit 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may ask for an explanation only for the last statement that Judge Greve has said. Because in this document I couldn't see that strong affiliation with the SDS and the JNA. I might have just missed. Please, if you could...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I should have been more explicit in stating that, at this point, I didn't quote the whole of it, but I am pleased to do so. "We have also supported the struggle of the patriotically committed members of the JNA in a war in which it was being deserted by its members, soldiers and officers up to the highest rank who had forgotten a whole list of all the duties of a patriot and a soldier to defend one's country. The SDS sent some of its best members to the battle field of Slovenia and Krajina. The party participated in mobilising and forming many battalion because the Serb people's patriotism obliged it. This is, therefore, the occasion to remind ourselves of the heroes of the Slovenian and other battle fields who sacrificed their lives for the survival of their nation." Said the chairman of the municipal SDS board, Ratko Mladic. I was summarising saying they were working together.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You were reading it from what page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The paragraph is on page 2 and it is the 4th paragraph. And if you've got it in cross-examination, you can cross-examine in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise, but I left my glasses in the locker room.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, is the document then admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, in your report at paragraphs 83 and 113, you discuss the creation of parallel or separate Serb administrative and political bodies. In that context, I would like to show you what we would ask be marked as Prosecution Exhibit 20 for identification. Could you tell us what that is, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a decision made by a parallel structure, the Serb People's Assembly in the Municipality of Prijedor. It's dated 17th of January, 1992. And it's a decision to unite with the Autonomous Region of the Bosanska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And, Dr. Greve, in your preparation for writing your report, can you tell us what you learned of the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina, what was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Initially, only from people, we learned that there were parallel structures that were being created, which were purely Serb and they were created inside of Prijedor. Very soon we also got information about official documents indicating the same. There was a special people's assembly of the Serb people in the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who decided in early 1992 to have a separate Serb republic, which would be a part of Yugoslavia, remain a part of Yugoslavia. And we also, little by little, learned there were other parallel structures, one of which was the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina region, which started to work as an independent entity which would take orders and work together with other Serb authorities, but not the elected authorities in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, this document, indicating a decision of the Serb People's Assembly of Prijedor to join this autonomous region of Bosanska Krajina, is that consistent with your analysis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We would offer this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would object. We would object to admission of this document. And we would object to this line of presentation of the Prosecutor's evidence. First, Your Honour, we have not heard this, the foundation of this document, whether Judge Greve has reviewed this document at the time when preparing the report, or before, while in the process of preparing a report. If she has not, that means she's not familiar with the document and the document should not be admitted. Secondly, if she had heard from the witnesses that the parallel government has been set up in Prijedor, she could also testify. But not to piggyback it on a document which is questionable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there any dispute, Mr. Vucicevic, about that aspect of the case that there were parallel structures? Is that matter in dispute or not? Are you arguing about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in dispute is what were the parallel structures that were established, who established them and whether the defendant was part thereof. And because the burden of proof is beyond a reasonable doubt, not be proven with specificity. What we're hearing here, a broad brush, I mean, what is objectionable to us is a statement on which, indeed, a learned jurist, it seems, but I would like to hear whether she has seen this document at the time, introduce the document, and she could testify on the document if that could be corroborated by other statements. But I think we are falling beyond the standards -- below the standards which we should be in this type of presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Hollis, perhaps the witness could deal with her knowledge of this document and the background of her knowledge of these matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour we would point out two things, however. First of all, the witness was asked whether this document was consistent with her analysis, not if she has used the document when preparing her report. And we believe as an expert, she can testify as to whether other evidence is consistent with her analysis and report. That's the first point. Secondly, Your Honour, we would ask if the Defence is questioning the authenticity of this document as a separate ground. Otherwise, it appears that the Defence is simply repeating arguments that have previously been overruled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's hear from the witness as to what she knows about this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the background of her knowledge of these events could be dealt with briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Consistent with the presiding Judge's request, would you please tell us, first of all, the document that you have before you, did you have this document at the time that you prepared your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not have it at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And, in that regard, I might ask you, what if any efforts you made in the preparation of your report to visit the area of Opstina Prijedor and to receive documents from the Serb officials there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did, the Commission of Experts, that is, did approach also the authorities in Belgrade, in Pale, everywhere, to see if we could have access to the area and if we could have access to documents. And the answer was, with one exception, always "no". The one exception that was made was that we were given the first draught of the constitution of what later became the Republika of Srpska. At that earlier time, it was the Republic of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So, save for that, we were not able to go -- I was not able to go to Prijedor. I was not able, although we made requests, to receive papers straight from the authorities. The official documents I got were, on occasional, small pieces, bits and pieces of information that some of the people who had left the area had with them. It was information which was reprinted in the local newspaper. There was information which was to be obtained from all sources, media reports, TV, radio. I should say that I do not speak the Serbo-Croat language, nor do I understand it. The occasional word, but nothing else. But I did actually receive a number of documents on the day when I was giving in my final version of the report about Prijedor. I had it faxed to me from an unknown source actually at that time. But it came out later these were authentic documents. And that was numerous documents coming from Banja Luka, from the Autonomous Region, that is. But, essentially, I was not able to get, sort of proper documents, step by step, to follow all that had happened. I had to get it by listening to, or rather, reading statements, asking people who had been to the area, looking at media sources and every available source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We shall admit this document. It will be a matter for us in due course to decide what weight we give these documents. We shall be inclined to admit them and then decide whether they are of considerable or no probative value. It is the practice of the Tribunal to admit all evidence, as I have said earlier, and to determine what probative value it has. We are not a jury. We are a Tribunal of professional judges and, on that basis, we tend to admit evidence and then weigh it. So, unless there are objections on different grounds, we shall be inclined to admit this sort of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The objections, basically, I do not object or ask you for a consideration or a ruling. I am just asking for a certain clearance here, Your Honour. Because these documents were obtained pursuant to this Court order, a warrant in search on the authorities in Banja Luka and Prijedor in December of the last year. And if such documents are obtained at that time, it should be so disclosed at the time they are being admitted. Then the proper inferences, even though professional judges, but if you do not receive timely, all the information, you are likely, indeed, with very slight probability, but you're likely sometimes to draw inferences which would be a more properly drawn, more timely connected if this information is given to you in the form of foundation. And I am not speaking -- I understand that elements of foundations are indeed very broad here, not as in the United States system where I practice. But, indeed, a certain foundation to these documents, we cannot sit here and allow the Prosecution to create the impression as if Judge Greve is testifying, having seen documents before. That is basically the import on our objections. We do not object as to whether or not if an officer sees this material all the time had come and testified. I have seized 1200 documents, here they are. These are originals. We don't mind, they can all be admitted. But the manner in what they're admitted now, that is creating the possibility for inferences that are not going to be proper. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I am not sure that I take that point. But the Prosecution could make clear when and where documents were obtained if they know, it may make matters easier.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In regard to this document, Your Honour, it was used in the Tadic case. It was obtained by an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor from the officials in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, in paragraphs 45 to 54 of your report, you discuss a population profile of Prijedor. And, in that discussion, you speak of the ethnic composition of the ethnic population of Prijedor. I would like to show you what is presently or what we would asked be marked as Prosecution Exhibit 21-A for identification. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the official results of the census for 1991. From then, the whole of Yugoslavia. But this is Bosnia and Herzegovina as a republic within that state.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, in your report, you have a listing of information and numbers about numbers of people in ethnic groups, what source did you use to arrive at that listing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, I had approached the diplomatic mission of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Geneva to provide me with this paper. They promised to give it to me, but I never got it in time. I did approach then the Croatian officials in Zagreb and asked for the same information. And I got a paper, which I thought would be exactly the same whether I had obtained it from the Croatian officials or from the Bosnia-Herzegovina officials. But, as it comes out, there may be small differences between the two documents. The one document I used, which originated from Zagreb, from Croatia, and this one document. But it's not even -- it's not large differences. But that goes to explain the difference between the figures you will find here and the figures that you will find in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you talk about it, it's not a large difference. Could you give the Trial Chamber some indication of the numbers that you're speaking of in terms of the difference, for example, in the overall population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am only speaking about very, very few. We are speaking in the overall numbers less than a hundred or approximately a hundred.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And if you could please turn to the portion of Prosecution Exhibit 21-A for identification that deals with the Prijedor area, beginning on page, at the bottom would indicate the last two digits, 21?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the total number will be 112,543.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I haven't got this. Which page are we on?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you would look at the English translation, at the bottom, the last two digits should be page 21, 22, 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And you noted a total population figure of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 112,543, which was then subdivided with the majority being 49,351 Muslims, approximately 44 per cent of the population; Serbs 47,581, approximately 42.5 per cent of the population; Croats, I am afraid I have difficulty in reading the figures, but it's 6,000, perhaps 500 something.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the proportion of the population that Croats made up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately 5.6 per cent, Your Honours. And then there is the group called "Yugoslavs." And any other ethnic or religious group might declare themselves as Yugoslavs. It could be because they had mixed descent. It could be because they wanted to state commitment to the Federation of Yugoslavia. So this may include people of different ethnic background. It's approximately the same size of that group as the one of Croats, it's 5.7 per cent of the population, approximately. And, finally, there would be a group called "others." Essentially, aliens. It would be Russians, Ukrainians, Italians, a few Poles. And that would be approximately 2.2 per cent of the population or 2,836 as listed in this paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, you've indicated that the figures you've given were somewhat different in that the overall amount was less than a hundred as far as the total population. The information that you were given, however, is this the same format in which it was given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Is it the same type of breakdown that this was given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would offer this as Prosecution Exhibit 21-A?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now. Is there any objection to this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, we will adjourn for a quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, before the recess we were talking about the population of Prijedor and the ethnic composition of that population, and you had reviewed a document 21A. I'd now ask that you look at a document we would ask be marked as 21B for Identification. Can you tell us what that is, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a continuation or another part of censuses. It's comparative censuses for several different years. It has also been provided by the Bosnian authorities. So I did not have them at the time I did my study, but I had similar information from the Croatian authorities at that time. An opstina, which is translated as a municipality or a district, is subdivided in Mjesna Zajednica, which is the next administrative unit. And what we have here is a breakdown within the Opstina, within the district or the municipality into the different, smaller administrative units, the Mjesna Zajednica for Prijedor area.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, for ease of review of these documents, if we turn to page -- the last three digits being 201, or page 196 is the other page designation. The indication there is "Prijedor." Is that where the breakdown of the Prijedor municipality begins?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Again, for ease of understanding this document, would it be correct to say that in reviewing the document we would take pages 201 and 202 and actually put them together as a longer sheet in reviewing the information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They will be printed in a book, a booklet, so that you can read them at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And the same would be true for pages 198 and 199, that is to say 203 and 204? You would also read those by putting them together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And do those pages continue with the breakdown of Opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And, finally, with pages 205 and 206, would you also read those in conjunction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I should add that starting a little below the middle of the page, on page 200, or 205, it starts with another opstina called Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, looking at the numbers for 1991 census, if you will, going back to the pages about Prijedor beginning on 201 and 202. What are the various categories that are listed under there, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, it is the total, the Croats, the Muslims, the Serbs, those who call themselves Yugoslavs, and a category of others.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And as we look at the headings above where we have Hrvati, Muslimani, Srbi, what are those categories, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the breakdown for each of the Mjesna Zajednica of the population composition as divided by these groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And if you go down those columns where they list the various groups reviewing that, could you tell us how frequently there would exist a village that would be totally one group or another?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's almost non-existent. People are living in mixed hamlets, essentially, and villages in the town of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And that mixture of people in virtually all the hamlets and villages and towns in Opstina Prijedor, is that consistent with your analysis of the population and the ethnic distribution of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would offer the exhibit as Prosecution Exhibit 21B. At this time I would like to have the witness be shown what we would ask be marked as Prosecution Exhibit 22 for Identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And what is that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a map which shows the Municipality of Prijedor, and almost in the heart of that is the town of Prijedor. It shows a simplification of the main group populating the different areas. But it's a simplification, as most areas will have mixed populations.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So that when it shows an area in a colour -- and could you tell us what the colour scheme is on the map, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the map the Serbs will be indicated with purple, the Muslims by green, and the Croats by yellow.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So then the respective colour for the group in an area is an indication of the predominant group in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We would offer that as Prosecution Exhibit 22.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: At this time I would like to show you what is marked on the exhibit list as Prosecution Exhibit 24 for Identification. And what is this, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a map. It's of Bosnia and Herzegovina with its subdivision and opstinas in district or municipalities, and some of the main towns are indicated as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And there's a colour scheme of green and pink on this map. Who prepared that colour scheme?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did. I did last night, actually. It is intended to visualise, again using green for the Muslims. Where there are opstinas which are predominantly Muslim, but far from only Muslim, it's Prijedor, it's Sanski Most and Kotor Varos. And there are a number of nearby opstinas which are marked with pink or red. And that, in this case, indicates a majority of Serbs, but again there were many non-Serbs in these areas as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And the greater area in which you have coloured these pink and green, is there any significance to that greater area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That greater area was what was to become the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: I would offer this exhibit as Prosecution Exhibit 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: We object to this exhibit, Your Honours. And the objection is that it would take a statistical expert to determine from the census reports which municipality had predominance over a population, because in the previous years, starting from '48 and going to '41, the group of citizens of Prijedor that we have seen have been changing, because a number of Muslims have been increasing and the number of Yugoslavs was decreasing, and then in certain census. So basically this conclusion could be not ethnic, but this was declaration of belonging to one or the other ethnic group, and also Yugoslavs was political declaration. So to admit this map -- a map without coloration we don't object, but map with coloration we do, because this witness is not qualified to make statistical analysis, nor political statements, that are basically that this map depicts. And that would be prejudicial to our client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Those are all matters which you can raise in cross-examination of the witness. Yes, we'll admit that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, based upon that objection, we would ask at this time that the witness be provided with an exhibit we had determined not to use, but now we'll ask to use. That is what we would ask to be marked as Prosecution Exhibit 23 for Identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, can you tell us what this map depicts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an ethnic map of the Republics of Croatia and of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: And if you could perhaps fold that map so that we are viewing the area in which Prijedor, Kotor Varos, the area that you were just referring to in the prior exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I need a copy of this exhibit. I didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You haven't got a copy?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've previously provided the Defence with a copy of the map. If they don't have it with them in the courtroom, we'll provide them a copy, but they had been provided with a copy of it. We do have --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Indeed, this beautiful colouring I would have noted. So if we can get a copy, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have we got a spare copy?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If we could ask to get this back after the examination. We will have another copy to replace it. But this is our remaining copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you could provide that to Defence Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, perhaps we would need to have the overhead brought in closer into the area of Banja Luka, Prijedor, Kotor Varos, the area you were just discussing. And is it possible to come in a little closer to that area? Dr. Greve, what do the various colours on that map depict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should, perhaps, explain a bit, because, as the Defence rightly pointed out, I have used, when I speak about Serbs, Muslims or Croats, or Yugoslavs, the way people have declared themselves in the census. I have not gone beyond it to ask what does it really mean to be a Serb or a Croat or a Muslim when they declare them that way. Meaning that I have not checked on the -- on what are the criteria. I have just noted that when people have declared themselves as belonging to one of these groups, that has been the basis for official statistics, and I have related to that official statistic. So that is the basis on which I have made a statement. This is actually Prijedor, and the circle and its subdivision reflects the different ethnic groups. We have the green for the Muslims, the purple for the Serbs, and the brownish colour is for the Yugoslavs, and the blue for the Croats, and the white one for the group of others. And as the previous map also was made, it's based on the same kind of official papers where I've not gone beyond what is the true nature of being Serb or Muslim. But again this is Sanski Most, and it's indicated that here that this is the population that's declared as Muslim, declared as Serb, aliens, and declared as -- or others, and declared as Croats. And we also have, when we come over to these areas, the Kotor Varos is there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Dr. Greve, the ethnic breakdown that relates to Prijedor that is shown on this map, is that consistent with your analysis of that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, but it's only one digit, like 2.2, et cetera. It's not exact. But it's close to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We would offer Prosecution Exhibit 23 for Identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Judge Greve, in your report you also discuss a plebiscite that was held by the Bosnian Serbs in November of 1991. And I believe you discussed that at paragraphs 98 to 102 of your report. Now, in that report you discuss different ballots that were used at that plebiscite. Could you tell us where you got your information for that discussion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was information I got from speaking to people who had actually voted in that plebiscite, and they told me that there were different colouring of two different ballot papers, one used for those who declared themselves as Serbs, and one used for others.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to be provided with what we would ask to be marked as Prosecution Exhibit 25 for Identification. And while that is being done, I would ask you, Dr. Greve, did you, at any time in preparing your report, actually see a copy of different ballots used in the plebiscite?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see the papers, but the wording was given to me. I had the wording and I wrote it down. It's in the report. But it was verbal transmission, oral transmission. I did not have it in writing. I did not see a ballot paper itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If you would look at that exhibit, please, and if you would tell us what it purports to be.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is actually, I believe, to save space, it's two different ballot papers that's been assembled on the same page, the first page. And there is then -- the first one is provided for people who declared themselves as Serbs, and the second half of the page below the dotted line was provided for those who were non-Serbs, and wanted to participate in the plebiscite. It was for everyone to participate in Bosnia-Herzegovina if they so wished, whether or not declared Serb or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Now, looking at the portion of the exhibit that is entitled "Instructions for conducting the plebiscite," if you could please look at the third page where it discusses voting.
